catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bulls-and-bri: This 1913 reference piece on bulls and briefs — the pope's solemn documents. Herbert Thurston explains their differing forms. The leaden seal marks the bull. The Fisherman's ring seals the brief. The chancery of the Holy See. Their forms fill the chancery's books.
coral-and-coral-reefs:
Thomas Henry Huxley delivered this lecture to explain what coral is and how reefs come to be. He begins with a distinction between the red coral of jewellery and babies' rattles and the white coral that builds in the sea. Both, he shows, are the internal skeletons of simple animals akin to the sea anemone.

The skeleton is carbonate of lime, the same stuff as limestone and the fur in a kettle, drawn out of sea water by the living polyp. Huxley builds from the single animal to the reef: how colonies grow, where they can live, and what their masses imply about the sea floor beneath them. It is a working naturalist's lecture, paced for a general audience, with the reef treated as evidence in a geological argument.
coral-reefs:
Charles Darwin published The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs from his Beagle voyage observations, and this text keeps his full title and plates list. Darwin sorts reefs into three kinds: atolls, the ring islands of open ocean; barrier reefs, which fence high islands at a distance; and fringing reefs, which skirt a shore. Keeling Atoll gets a chapter of close description, from its zones of coral to the fish that eat them.

His fifth chapter argues the famous theory: as an island slowly sinks, its fringing reef grows upward into a barrier, then an atoll, so reef shape records the sea floor's motion. Maps of reef distribution test the idea worldwide. It was Darwin's first great geological book, bold long before the species theory.
podcast-tuckercarlson-4PkEwKz0Pfs:
Tucker Carlson's podcast takes up a Christian prayer app with an odd pair of facts attached: it was banned in China and backed by actor Mark Wahlberg. The segment treats the app as a small story that opens onto a big one about faith and state power.

Carlson looks at why a prayer tool would draw a ban, and what its growth says about hunger for daily prayer in a loud age. The Wahlberg link shows how star support moves such products into the mainstream. The talk mixes tech, religion, and free speech, and it keeps coming back to who gets to limit belief.
pointed-roofs:
Dorothy M. Richardson published Pointed Roofs in London with Duckworth, and a second impression followed in 1921. The book, dedicated to Winifred Ray, opens with an introduction describing three readings of the manuscript, in handwriting, in typescript. In print, and wrestling with whether the work is realism or the most subjective thing its reader had ever read. That argument is the novel in miniature: a young woman's consciousness, registered from inside.

Richardson's heroine goes to teach in Germany, and the story renders her sensations, embarrassments, and small illuminations as they happen, without the scaffolding of conventional plot. Pointed Roofs became the first volume of the long Pilgrimage sequence and a founding text of stream-of-consciousness fiction in English, written in parallel with Joyce and before Woolf's major work. The introduction's honest puzzlement preserves the shock of first contact with a genuinely new way of writing a life.
the-scottish-chiefs:
Miss Jane Porter opens The Scottish Chiefs with a chapter simply headed Scotland. The summer of 1296 was bright, she writes. The war that had desolated Scotland was then at an end. Vanquished Scots hoped they might wear their chains in peace. Noblemen had signed a bond of submission to a ruthless conqueror that spring.

Edward the First of England had entered Scotland with an immense army. He seized Berwick by stratagem and laid the country in ashes. At Dunbar he forced the Scottish king to acknowledge him liege lord. One brave man's spirit remained unsubdued, though. William Wallace retired to the glen of Ellerslie, disgusted at the submission. Too noble to bend to the usurper, he gave up the world. He sought resignation to evils he could not redress, Porter writes.
